pos: n. (Hessian town on the Lahn; seat of the first Protestant university, of the colloquy of 1529, and of the Reformed reform of 1605)
etymology: German Marburg, from Mark, a boundary, and Burg, a fortified place—the border castle above the Lahn.
biblical_def: Marburg holds three places in the history of the Reformation. In 1527 Landgrave Philip of Hesse founded there the first university established as a Protestant foundation, which trained the ministry of Hesse and of much of central Germany. In October 1529 the same prince brought Luther and Zwingli, with Melanchthon, Bucer, Oecolampadius and others, to his castle to settle the quarrel over the Lord's Supper; they agreed on fourteen articles and parted on the fifteenth, and the Protestant division dates from that room. Then in 1605 Landgrave Moritz the Learned, having concluded that the Reformed doctrine was the biblical one, imposed on Hesse-Kassel the measures called the points of improvement: the images taken out of the churches, the Decalogue restored to its Reformed numbering so that the second commandment stood alone, and the bread broken in the Supper. The Lutheran professors of Marburg refused, were removed, and went to found Giessen, so that one Hessian university became two confessions. The dictionary enters Marburg because all three of its episodes are about the same thing: whether the plain words of Scripture govern the church's worship, and what it costs when two parties both answer yes and disagree about what the words say.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colloquy as a conference, a mutual discourse; a university as a corporation for instruction in all the branches of learning; and improvement as advancement in anything good.
webster_full: COLLOQUY, n. [L. colloquium.] Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; conference; a dialogue.
UNIVERSITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
IMPROVEMENT, n. Advancement in any thing good or valuable; a making or growing better; the act of amending.
ARTICLE, n. A single clause in a contract or system of regulations; a point of faith distinctly stated.
DIVISION, n. [L. divisio.] The act of dividing; the state of being divided; discord; variance; disagreement.

corruption_summary: Hessian town of the first Protestant university, of the 1529 colloquy on the Supper, and of the Reformed points of improvement of 1605.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine controversy is the fifteenth article, and the dictionary states its position rather than lamenting the division. On the Supper it holds, with the Reformed, that the bread and wine are a sign and seal in which Christ is truly present to the believer by faith and by the Spirit, and it rejects transubstantiation, the Lutheran sacramental union, and the bare memorialism which denies the spiritual presence. The Marburg parting was therefore not a failure of charity on either side but a real difference about the nature of a sacrament, and it could not have been papered over.

The principle to recover is the second commandment in its own right. “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) stands as a separate commandment and is not a clause of the first; the medieval numbering which folded it into the first and split the tenth is the numbering under which the churches filled with images. Moritz's restoring of the Reformed order in 1605 was right, and the manner—a prince imposing a confession on professors and parishes—was the standing fault of the German second reformations.

pos: n. (capital of Hesse-Kassel; where Landgrave Moritz the Learned brought the landgraviate to the Reformed confession in 1605)
etymology: German Kassel, recorded as Chassalla, probably from Latin castellum, a fort, or a Germanic cassel, a settlement by the ford of the Fulda.
biblical_def: Kassel was the residence of the landgraves of Hesse and became, under Moritz the Learned, the capital of a Reformed state. Moritz, who ruled from 1592, was a prince of real learning—a musician who composed, a patron of mathematics and astronomy, the founder of a court school for the nobility—and he came by study to the conviction that the Reformed doctrine of the Supper and the Reformed reading of the second commandment were the biblical ones. In 1605 he published the points of improvement for his lands and enforced them: images and altars removed from the churches, the Decalogue taught in the Reformed numbering, the bread broken at the Supper, and subscription required of the clergy and the professors. Those who refused lost their places. The reform was genuine, it was resented, and it was one of the causes which drew Hesse-Kassel into the Thirty Years War on the Protestant side, at a cost which included Moritz's own abdication in 1627. The dictionary enters Kassel because the episode states both halves of the German problem exactly: a prince used his authority to establish a truer doctrine, and in doing so confirmed the principle that a prince's authority is the proper instrument for settling doctrine, which is the error that would later be used against the gospel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a landgrave as a German count having jurisdiction over a territory; subscription as the act of signing one's name in assent; and reformation as a change from worse to better, an amendment of life or doctrine.
webster_full: LANDGRAVE, n. [G. land and grave, a count.] In Germany, a count or earl; a nobleman having jurisdiction over a territory.
SUBSCRIPTION, n. The act of subscribing; the signing of one's name, as in token of consent or attestation.
REFORMATION, n. [L. reformatio.] Change from worse to better; amendment of life or manners; in church history, the great change of religion in the sixteenth century.
ALTAR, n. [L. altare.] A mount; an elevation of earth, stone or other matter, on which sacrifices were offered.
ABDICATE, v.t. [L. abdico.] To abandon; particularly, to relinquish an office or sovereignty before the term of service has expired.

Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:

corruption_summary: Hessian capital where Moritz the Learned enforced the Reformed points of improvement in 1605, removing images and requiring the clergy to subscribe.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is not the doctrine Moritz established, which the dictionary holds, but the instrument he used. The territorial principle—that a prince settles the religion of his land—makes the magistrate the judge of doctrine, and a magistrate who may command the removal of images may also command their restoration; in Bentheim a generation later one did. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) establishes the civil office and does not hand it the keys of the church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the second commandment and the regulative principle it implies. “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it” (Hab 2:18) is the prophet's question, and the answer the churches of Europe had given for centuries was that it profited the devotion of the simple. It did not. The dictionary commends the clearing of the Hessian churches and holds that it ought to have been done by the churches themselves, upon conviction, with the prince protecting the work rather than decreeing it.

pos: n. (county town on the Main; where a new town was built in 1597 for Walloon and Dutch Reformed refugees)
etymology: German Hanau, from Hagen, an enclosure or hedged place, and Aue, a water-meadow; the town stands where the Kinzig enters the Main.
biblical_def: Hanau was the seat of the counts of Hanau-Munzenberg, east of Frankfurt on the Main, and in 1597 Count Philipp Ludwig the Second did something few princes of the Empire were willing to do: he invited the Reformed refugees of the Netherlands and the Walloon provinces into his territory, granted them a charter, and laid out beside his old town an entire new town for them to build and inhabit. The Neustadt of Hanau was planned on a grid, given its own magistracy and its own French and Dutch Reformed congregations, and filled with the trades the refugees brought—cloth, silk, goldsmithing, printing, jewelling—so that within a generation it was richer than the town it had been added to. A Latin school of standing was founded, and the Hanau presses printed Reformed and Hebrew books for the whole region. The dictionary enters Hanau as the best instance in Germany of a policy which was both obedience and good sense. “Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11) describes the people who came; the count who received them did what the law of God requires toward the stranger, and was enriched in the doing of it, which is the ordinary way of that commandment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refugee as one who flees for shelter; a charter as a written instrument granting rights; and an artisan as one skilled in a manual art.
webster_full: REFUGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who in times of persecution flees to a foreign country.
CHARTER, n. [L. charta.] A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or of rights and privileges.
ARTISAN, n. [Fr.] One trained to manual dexterity in some mechanic art or trade; a handicraftsman; a mechanic.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; a guest; one not a member of the family.
SETTLE, v.t. To place in a fixed state; to establish in an abode or in a calling; to plant with inhabitants.
scriptures: Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
corruption_summary: Main valley county town where a whole new town was laid out in 1597 for Walloon and Dutch Reformed refugees, with its own charter and congregations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary refuses two readings of this episode. The first is the merely economic, which treats the refugee charters of Hanau, Frankfurt and Emden as early industrial policy and leaves out the reason the people were homeless; the second is the merely sentimental, which treats them as pure charity and leaves out that the counts knew exactly what a Flemish weaver was worth. Both halves were true at Hanau, and the biblical categories hold both without embarrassment.

The principle to recover is the law of God concerning the stranger, in the precise form Scripture gives it. The biblical categories are the stranger, the sojourner, the widow and the fatherless—people in a named and concrete condition, owed named and concrete duties. “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land” (Psa 137:4) is what the exile asks; a charter, a plot of ground and a congregation of his own language is the answer a Christian magistrate can give, and Hanau gave it.

pos: n. (county of the house of Nassau in the Westerwald; made Reformed by Count John the Sixth, who founded the academy of Herborn)
etymology: Nassau, from the family seat on the Lahn, nass, wet, and Aue, a meadow; Dillenburg, the castle on the river Dill.
biblical_def: The county of Nassau-Dillenburg lay in the hill country of the Westerwald, and its importance is out of all proportion to its size, for two reasons. The first is the family. William of Orange, who led the Dutch revolt, was born at Dillenburg, and his brother John the Sixth, who ruled the county for fifty years, supported that revolt with money, men and diplomacy throughout. The second is the church. John the Sixth brought his lands from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession in the 1570s, issued a church order in 1582 drawn on the Dutch and Palatine models with consistories and discipline, and in 1584 founded the high school at Herborn, which under Olevianus, Piscator, Zepper and Alsted became one of the great Reformed academies of Europe and trained ministers for Hungary, Bohemia, Poland, the Netherlands and the German counties. A county of a few market towns in the hills therefore furnished the Dutch Republic with its first stadholder and the Reformed world with a seminary. The dictionary enters Nassau-Dillenburg because it is the plainest proof that in the providence of God the usefulness of a church is not measured by the size of the territory it occupies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an academy as a school for the instruction of youth in the higher branches; a consistory as an ecclesiastical court; and discipline as government and correction, as of a church.
webster_full: ACADEMY, n. [Gr. from Academia, a garden near Athens.] A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.
CONSISTORY, n. An assembly of ecclesiastical persons for the regulation of church affairs; a spiritual court.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules; correction; chastisement; the system of a church's order.
COUNTY, n. A circuit or portion of a kingdom into which the whole is divided for the purposes of government.
SEMINARY, n. A place of education; a school for the training of ministers or teachers.

Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
corruption_summary: Small Nassau county whose count turned it Reformed in the 1570s, ordered its churches in 1582, and founded the academy of Herborn in 1584.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the measuring of churches by scale, which is as old as the census David was punished for taking and as modern as the conference platform. Nassau-Dillenburg had perhaps a few tens of thousands of souls. It produced a church order copied across Germany, an academy whose students carried the Reformed divinity into five countries, and the house that held the Netherlands together through forty years of war.

The principle to recover is the apostle's division of labour. “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) assigns men the planting and the watering and reserves the increase; and a count who founds a school is planting something whose fruit he will not live to count. The dictionary holds that this is the ordinary shape of useful work in the kingdom, and that a generation which insists on seeing its own harvest will plant nothing worth harvesting.

pos: n. (Nassau town in the Westerwald; the second seat of the Nassau high school, moved between Siegen and Herborn)
etymology: German Siegen, from the river Sieg, a name of early Germanic or Celtic origin; the town lies in the iron country of the Westerwald.
biblical_def: Siegen was the second town of the Nassau counties, set in the iron and charcoal country of the Westerwald, and the residence of the Nassau-Siegen branch of the house. Its place in church history is as the companion and sometimes the rival of Herborn: the Nassau high school, founded at Herborn in 1584, was moved to Siegen and back again more than once in its first decades as war, plague and family division required, so that a student of the 1590s might take part of his course in one town and part in the other. Count John the Seventh of Nassau-Siegen maintained the Reformed church order he had inherited and also founded a military academy at Siegen, the first of its kind in Europe, to train officers for the Dutch service. The town was afterwards divided between a Reformed and, from the middle of the seventeenth century, a Catholic line of the family, each holding part of the same small territory. The dictionary enters Siegen for the itinerant school, which is a useful corrective. An institution is not its building. The Nassau academy did its work while being carried back and forth across twenty miles of hill country, because what it consisted of was a library, four or five professors, and a conviction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines itinerant as wandering, not settled; a professor as one who publicly teaches a science; and a library as a collection of books belonging to a person or society.
webster_full: ITINERANT, adj. [L. iter, a journey.] Passing or traveling about a country; wandering; not settled; applied to a preacher or teacher.
PROFESSOR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; an officer in a university or college.
LIBRARY, n. [L. librarium.] A collection of books belonging to a private person or to a public institution or a company.
FOUNDRY, n. [Fr. fonderie.] The art of casting metals; a house or works where founding is carried on.
ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning; a society of men united for the promotion of arts or science.

For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
corruption_summary: Nassau town which shared the Herborn high school by turns, and whose count founded the first military academy in Europe for the Dutch service.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the identification of a church or a school with its premises, which is a chronic Protestant failing in a tradition that officially denies it. Congregations split over buildings, colleges decline when their endowment is spent on architecture, and a denomination will hold an empty shell for a century because the deeds are in its name. Siegen and Herborn between them held one academy in two places and it was the same academy.

The principle to recover is the one Scripture states of the whole church and which applies to its institutions: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). A school that can be moved is a school that can survive a war. The dictionary also records the military academy without enthusiasm and without disdain: a Reformed count training officers for the Dutch service was doing a lawful work of the civil sphere, and it is not the same work as the ministry.

pos: n. (principality on the middle Elbe and Saale, brought from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession about 1596)
etymology: German Anhalt, from the castle of Anhalt in the Harz, the name read as an Halt, at the holding or the stronghold.
biblical_def: Anhalt was a small principality on the middle Elbe and Saale, divided among the sons of Joachim Ernst into the lines of Dessau, Bernburg, Plotzkau, Kothen and Zerbst, and it is the clearest German case of a Lutheran territory going over to the Reformed confession by the conviction of its princes. Joachim Ernst had already been drawn toward the Melanchthonian side; his sons, chiefly Johann Georg and Christian, completed the change about 1596, adopting the Reformed doctrine of the Supper, removing images and the remaining Lutheran ceremonies, and ordering the churches on the Palatine model. Anhalt produced a confession of its own and maintained a Reformed church into the modern period, and its princes were active in the Protestant Union which preceded the Thirty Years War—Christian of Anhalt-Bernburg commanded the Bohemian army at the White Mountain in 1620 and lost it. The dictionary enters Anhalt for the shape of the change. It was argued in the universities, decided in a family, and imposed on the parishes; the doctrine adopted was the truer one, and the method made the doctrine look like a dynastic preference, which is the reason the Lutheran population of such territories resisted longest where it had been catechised best.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a principality as the territory of a prince; a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; and conformity as compliance with an established form.
webster_full: PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; the territory of a prince, or the country which gives title to a prince; a prince's dominion.
CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a public acknowledgment of belief.
CONFORMITY, n. Compliance with an established form, rule or practice, particularly in religion; correspondence with a pattern.
CEREMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion; the outward forms of worship.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest or minister; the inhabitants of such a district.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
corruption_summary: Elbe principality carried from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession about 1596 by the conviction of its princes and the order of their church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary holds the doctrine Anhalt adopted. On the Supper it confesses a sign and seal in which Christ is truly present to faith, and rejects the Lutheran sacramental union as well as the Roman change of substance; on images it holds the second commandment as a commandment and not a gloss. Where it differs from the Anhalt princes is on the instrument, and the difference is not small: a confession received by a church is a confession, and a confession decreed for a church is a policy.

The principle to recover is that conviction cannot be delegated. “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught” (2Th 2:15) is said to a congregation, and the congregations of Anhalt were told in 1596 which traditions they had been taught. The dictionary notes the irony that followed: the princely house which had reasoned its way to the Reformed confession went on to stake the Protestant cause on a battle outside Prague and lose it in an afternoon.

pos: n. (Anhalt residence town; seat of a Reformed high school and of the printing of the Anhalt church books)
etymology: German Zerbst, from a Slavic form Ciervisti, a place of the Serbian or Sorbian people who held the Elbe country before the German settlement.
biblical_def: Zerbst was the chief town of the Anhalt-Zerbst line and the place where the principality's church learning and church printing were concentrated. Its high school, refounded on the buildings of a dissolved Franciscan house in the later sixteenth century, was a gymnasium illustre of the kind the small Reformed states depended on: it taught Latin, Greek, Hebrew, logic and theology, prepared men for Herborn, Heidelberg or Leiden, and served families who could not send a boy abroad at fourteen. The town's presses printed the Anhalt church order, the catechisms, hymnbooks and the confession by which the principality defined its position after the change of 1596. Zerbst was also, in the way of small residence towns, the place where that position was most visible: a court, a school, a press and three or four churches within a few streets, all under one family's patronage, so that a change of mind in the castle appeared in the schoolroom within a year. The dictionary enters Zerbst for both sides of that closeness, which gave a small Reformed state its coherence and left it no second opinion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gymnasium as a high school preparatory to the university; a patron as one who supports or protects; and a hymnbook as a collection of hymns for public worship.
webster_full: GYMNASIUM, n. In Germany, a high school or seminary of learning preparatory to the university; a place of exercise.
PATRON, n. One who countenances, supports or protects; a guardian; one who has the gift of a church living.
HYMNBOOK, n. A collection of hymns, usually for the use of a congregation in public worship.
COURT, n. The residence of a prince; the persons who compose the retinue of a sovereign; a judicatory.
COHERENCE, n. [L. cohaerentia.] A sticking together; connection; consistency; suitable connection of parts.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Anhalt residence town whose high school and presses supplied the principality's ministers, catechisms, hymnbooks and church order.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the single patron. Where a court, a school, a press and the parishes all depend on one family, there is no place in the territory from which the family can be contradicted, and the uniformity which looks like health is the absence of any possible second opinion. The dictionary names this as a structural fault of the small confessional state, and notes that it is reproduced in miniature wherever one donor funds a church's building, staff and publishing at once.

The principle to recover is the Berean duty, which assumes a people able to check their teachers: “they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). The congregation that cannot do the searching, or cannot afford the answer it might find, has lost something the printing of catechisms will not replace. The schools and presses of Zerbst were a real good, and they were not a substitute for that.

pos: n. (Anhalt residence town at the junction of the Mulde and the Elbe; seat of the senior Anhalt line)
etymology: German Dessau, from a Slavic root dessa, a settlement, with German Aue, a water-meadow; the town lies where the Mulde joins the Elbe.
biblical_def: Dessau was the residence of the senior line of the princes of Anhalt, standing where the Mulde runs into the Elbe in the flat country between Wittenberg and Magdeburg, and it has a double claim on the dictionary's attention. The first is that this was the Lutheran heartland: Wittenberg lies a short ride upstream, Luther preached in the town, and the Anhalt princes had been among the earliest to receive the Reformation in its Lutheran form—the League of Dessau, formed here in 1525, was a league of Catholic princes against it, which marks how early the question was joined. The second is that the same house carried its lands over to the Reformed confession at the end of the century, so that Dessau became a Reformed court within sight of Lutheran Saxony. The result was a long, close and ill-tempered neighbourhood, in which the two confessions argued across a provincial border about the Supper, the images and the breaking of the bread, each with its own university behind it. The dictionary enters Dessau for that neighbourhood, because the Protestant division is usually described between nations and was in fact lived like this: two towns a day apart, two catechisms, one language.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a league as an alliance between princes or states; a neighbourhood as the inhabitants who live near; and controversy as a dispute carried on in writing.
webster_full: LEAGUE, n. [Fr. ligue.] An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense; a combination.
NEIGHBORHOOD, n. A place near; vicinity; the inhabitants who live in the vicinity of each other.
CONTROVERSY, n. [L. controversia.] A disputation, particularly in writing; a dispute concerning a matter of opinion.
BORDER, n. The outer edge of any thing; the exterior limit of a country or jurisdiction; a frontier.
CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
corruption_summary: Senior Anhalt residence beside Lutheran Saxony, which became a Reformed court and argued the Supper across a provincial border for generations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of calling the Lutheran and Reformed difference a misunderstanding of language. It was not. The Lutheran confession holds the body and blood of Christ to be truly and substantially present in, with and under the bread and wine, and received by the mouth of the unbeliever as well as the believer; the Reformed confession denies both, and holds Christ truly present to the believer by faith and by the Spirit. Those are contrary propositions and no formula reconciles them.

The principle to recover is the manner of the quarrel rather than its existence. “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) prescribes doctrine as the instrument; two courts a day apart conducted the argument for a century largely by pamphlet, insult and the exclusion of each other's students. The dictionary holds that the difference is real, that the Reformed side of it is the biblical one, and that the way it was carried on at Dessau and Wittenberg disgraced both.

pos: n. (Beuthen on the Oder in Silesia, Polish Bytom Odrzanski; seat of a Reformed high school founded in 1601 and suppressed in 1629)
etymology: German Beuthen, from a Slavic root, Polish Bytom, a dwelling-place; distinguished as Odrzanski, on the Oder, from the Upper Silesian town of the same name.
biblical_def: Beuthen on the Oder was a small Silesian town whose lord, Georg von Schonaich, founded there in 1601 a high school which bore his name and which was, for a generation, the chief Reformed academy of the Silesian and Polish borderland. It was generously endowed, it had a library and a press, it drew professors from Germany and students from Silesia, Poland, Hungary and Bohemia, and it taught the Reformed divinity in a province that was overwhelmingly Lutheran and under a Catholic Habsburg crown. That position was its death. In the Counter-Reformation which followed the imperial victories of the 1620s the school was suppressed, in 1629, and the territory brought back to the old religion; the library was dispersed and the professors scattered to Brandenburg, the Netherlands and Hungary. It had lasted twenty-eight years. The dictionary enters Beuthen because so short a life is a real question. A man spent a fortune on a school which was closed within his lifetime, and the honest account has to say both that the fortune was not wasted—the men it trained preached for forty years in four countries—and that the institution itself was lost and never restored.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to endow as to settle a permanent fund upon; to suppress as to put down, to crush; and dispersion as the state of being scattered.
webster_full: ENDOW, v.t. [L. dos, a dowry.] To furnish with a portion of estate; to settle a permanent fund or dower upon, as a school or church.
SUPPRESS, v.t. [L. suppressus.] To crush; to subdue; to put an end to; to prohibit, as the exercise of a religion.
DISPERSION, n. The act of scattering; the state of being scattered or separated into remote parts.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a permanent fund for the support of an institution; the fund so settled.
LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a person or to an institution; a building appropriated to such a collection.
scriptures: Act 8:1

And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
corruption_summary: Silesian town whose richly endowed Reformed academy of 1601 was suppressed in 1629, its library dispersed and its professors scattered.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the suppression itself: a state deciding that a school of the wrong confession should not exist, and closing it. It was done by the law of the land and it is the same act, in a quieter form, as the closing of the Eperjes collegium or the taking of the Marburg chairs; and the dictionary names all three as persecution, including the one carried out by a Reformed prince against Lutheran professors. A confession established by removing the other party's teachers has proved nothing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the fruitfulness of scattering. “And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad” (Act 8:1) is followed in the next verses by the preaching of the word wherever the scattered went. Beuthen's professors went to Brandenburg, the Netherlands and Hungary and taught there. The dictionary holds that this is a mercy and not a vindication of the men who caused it, and that the loss of the school was a real loss which the mercy does not cancel.

pos: n. (Christoph Pezel, 1539–1604, Philippist expelled from Wittenberg, who brought the city of Bremen to the Reformed confession)
etymology: Pezel, a south German surname, probably a diminutive of Peter; Christoph, from Greek Christophoros, one who bears Christ.
biblical_def: Christoph Pezel was a professor at Wittenberg of the party called Philippist, which followed Melanchthon in holding a doctrine of the Lord's Supper nearer the Reformed than the Lutheran. When the Elector of Saxony turned against that party in 1574 Pezel was imprisoned and then expelled, with others, in the affair the Lutheran historians call the crypto-Calvinist crisis; it was the moment at which Lutheranism closed its ranks and the Philippists had to become Reformed or be silent. Pezel went to Nassau, served the counts there, and in 1581 was called to Bremen, where he spent the rest of his life. Bremen had been Lutheran, and under Pezel's teaching and preaching the city went over, formally and gradually, to the Reformed confession; he drew up the Bremen Consensus of 1595, which set out that position, and he founded the city's gymnasium illustre, which trained its ministers thereafter. He died in 1604. The dictionary enters Pezel because the Philippists are a lost party worth remembering: men who believed they were being faithful to Melanchthon and to the Augsburg Confession rightly read, who were thrown out for it, and who found when they looked for a home that the only church which would confess what they already held was the Reformed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a consensus as agreement, concurrence; to expel as to drive out, to banish; and a party as a number of persons united in opinion.
webster_full: CONSENT, n. [L. consensus.] Agreement of minds; accord; concurrence; unity of opinion.
EXPEL, v.t. [L. expello.] To drive or force out; to eject; to banish; to exclude from a society or community.
PARTY, n. [Fr. partie.] A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community.
CRYPTO, a Greek prefix signifying hidden or secret; used in composition, as crypto-Calvinist, a secret Calvinist.
GRADUAL, adj. [L. gradus, a step.] Proceeding by steps or degrees; advancing step by step; slow.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Act 8:1

And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.
Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: Wittenberg Philippist expelled in 1574 who brought Bremen to the Reformed confession, drew its Consensus of 1595 and founded its high school.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary states plainly where it stands on the quarrel that made Pezel. The Philippists held that Christ is present in the Supper to the faith of the believer and not in, with and under the elements to the mouth of all; that is the Reformed doctrine, and it is the dictionary's. The charge of crypto-Calvinism was therefore substantially accurate, and the fault in the proceeding was not the identification but the method: imprisonment and expulsion of professors for a doctrine, by a prince, on a party's complaint.

The principle to recover is that a man under pressure must say what he believes. The Philippists' weakness before 1574 was ambiguity—holding the Reformed sense while subscribing formulas their colleagues read the Lutheran way—and the crisis simply ended the ambiguity. “no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) is the standard. Pezel came out of it clearer than he went in, and gave Bremen a confession in plain words and a school to teach it.
